extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and literate readers of poetry and prose (literary friends/colleagues)
extracted.subtask_description: Epistolary literary criticism and aesthetic remarks about poetry, narrative, and criticism (Romantic-period context). Lamb's letters articulate what he sees as virtues and faults in poems, novels, and critical behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / independence from sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem (or epic) should not be merely a verbal copying of an earlier master; it must have its own original incidents and lines rather than borrow incidents and speeches wholesale (Lamb's complaint about Wilkie's 'Epigoniad' being 'every incident and speech borrowed from Homer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criticism: Wilkie's epic 'in which there is not one tolerable good line all through, but every incident and speech borrowed from Homer.' Implied rule: avoid wholesale imitation; strive for genuine invention even within traditional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of individual lines / readable versification
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should possess at least 'tolerable good lines' throughout; sustaining arresting or tolerably good lines matters more than vast quantity (Lamb on an eight-thousand-line epic with nothing good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit scoring note: length alone (e.g., eight thousand lines) does not guarantee merit; evaluate by the presence of effective lines and passages rather than bulk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness and naturalness of idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases and constructions should conform to natural English usage; awkward constructions (e.g., 'one a man' instead of 'a man', 'he the king' instead of 'the king') mark defective diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb points to Cottle's peculiar uses as defects: 'Instead of a man,... he constantly writes "one a man"... Instead of the king... he constantly writes "he the king".' Guidance: favor idiomatic, unobtrusive phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in sensationalism / tonal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid piling on horrific or terrific images indiscriminately; excesses of frightful or sensational detail (serpents, spiders, ghosts, dead bodies, staircases made of nothing) break plausibility and tire the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb's mock of Cottle: 'His terrific scenes are indefatigable... Serpents, asps, spiders, ghosts, dead bodies, staircases made of nothing...' Use moderation and maintain consistent tone and dramatic plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and editing (economy of detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer must select among impressions; avoid presenting 'all' without discrimination — originality without selection results in undistinguished mass-description ('there is originality in it ... but no _selection. All_ is, described').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: choose what to include; omit redundant or undifferentiated description. Lamb praises 'beautiful, bare narratives' for their restraint (Robinson Crusoe, Vicar of Wakefield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't lecture — avoid didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'teach' the reader by direct instruction; 'instructions conveyed... are too direct, and like a lecture' insult an intelligent reader by telling them where and how to feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sign-posting feelings ('Let not my reader suppose', 'I will teach you how to think'); instead let the narrative and imagery enable the reader to infer. Lamb contrasts modern writers who 'put a sign-post up to show where you are to feel' with artists who trust the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust the reader — implicit compact
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an 'unwritten compact between author and reader: "I will tell you a story, and I suppose you will understand it."' Authors should assume reasonable intelligence and not overexplain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic guidance: favor implicitness and economy; do not dilute narrative force with unnecessary explanations, prologues, or apologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'affected' or overblown style
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of an 'affected' manner — artificial ornament or forced rhetorics (what Longinus and Dionysius Halicarnassus call 'the affected') that call attention to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-correction: Lamb notes when he himself is sliding into the affected; guidance is to watch for mannerisms and prefer natural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate titling / paratextual honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Paratext (titles, descriptive labels) should not undercut the work's intended effect or truth — e.g., calling the 'Ancient Mariner' a 'Poet's Reverie' diminishes the tale's claim to truth and reduces its force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use titles that disclaim or weaken the reader's acceptance of the narrative; let the tale's form and title work to enhance, not undermine, its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve necessary universality / avoid unnecessary specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain tales, retaining anonymity or lack of fixed profession (no character and profession) can strengthen the work's effect by removing distracting individuality and enhancing the dreamlike/universal quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb argues the 'Ancient Mariner' ought not to have had a detailed character/profession because the trials overwhelm individuality; consider whether specificity aids or detracts from the tale's intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse, needless satire that mars poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarse or trivial satire (e.g., 'common satire upon parsons and lawyers' or coarse epithets) can disfigure an otherwise fine poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sparing and tasteful with satirical lines; watch for words or jibes that jar with the poem's tone ('Poet's Epitaph' disfigured to Lamb by such moments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical discernment — don't praise indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should possess discernment rather than assume every work or author is a 'fine genius'; indiscriminate approbation (George's view that 'All poems are _good_ poems') is a failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate judgment and be able to distinguish merit from mere good intentions; friends who praise everything give poor guidance. Context-sensitive kindness aside, honest appraisal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity in giving criticism (adjust to context)
rubrics_metrics.description: When delivering criticism, consider the audience and circumstances — Lamb deliberately gave flattering praise to a grieving author to console him ('I made shift to discuss the most essential parts entirely to the satisfaction of its author').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical note: blunt candour is not always the best policy socially; balance candour with humanity and choose whether to be candid or consoling depending on occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and concision as marks of a good conversational/writing hand
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pleasant hand' or good writer is 'the clearest-headed fellow; fullest of matter, with least verbosity' — clarity and richness without verbosity are virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for fullness of matter (substance) combined with economy of language; being 'up to anything, down to everything' implies versatile, lucid expression without unnecessary prolixity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explanatory prologues that spoil wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not add prose apologies or explanatory prefaces that 'open the eyes of dead men that cannot see' — such prefaces can weaken the tale's mysterious or uncanny power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the narrative evoke wonder or mystery; resist defensive or reductive paratext that explains away effects meant to be experienced.
